alternatives.argument: Saturation of open unions of leaves is standard leaf vocabulary: the item's strategy unfolds the published definitions of regular foliation atlas and leaf, and the Leiden notes §1.3.6 (Definition 1.19, tangency of a foliation to a submanifold) records the same notion. Nothing beyond the published DG items is used.

The finite-intersection construction in the item's strategy reproduces MMF §2.3's first step completely: finitely many representatives are chosen on a common neighbourhood and the invariant domain is formed by a finite intersection; the Leiden notes Theorem 2.13's proof sketch performs the same shrinking. Only finiteness of the holonomy group and the germ group are used.

The normal model is constructed on this page from the holonomy cover and the quotient-foliation proposition; del Hoyo–Fernandes §2 states the same model (L'×R^q)/H' as the linearization of Reeb stability, and the Leiden notes §2.2 gives the finite-holonomy statement from which the model is assembled. The construction uses the deck-group identification and the quotient foliation.

Complete proof route assembled from the scaffolded lemmas: the model map is well defined and equivariant, is a foliated local diffeomorphism, and restricts to a diffeomorphism onto a saturated neighbourhood; the statement is corroborated independently by del Hoyo–Fernandes §1–2 (linearization form), Santos §§1–2 (tubular/retracting form with finite coverings) and the Leiden notes Theorem 2.13. The spherical-leaf case is proved in full in Calegari Theorem 4.5 and in Mrowka §§23.3–23.4.

When the holonomy representation is trivial, ker ρ = π1(L), so the holonomy cover is the identity cover and the model of the item is the product L×D; local Reeb stability then gives the product neighbourhood. This is the classical trivial-holonomy case, stated in the Leiden notes §2.2 and in Santos §2, and it needs no source beyond the local theorem.

A homomorphic image of a finite group is finite, so finiteness of π1(L) implies finiteness of the holonomy image and the local theorem applies; the non-necessity is exhibited by product foliations with infinite π1 (companion counterexample). The argument uses only the holonomy representation and the local theorem.

Global form assembled from the scaffolded items: openness of the compact-diffeomorphic-leaf set, closedness by the Novikov/Calegari limit argument, and the bundle-structure lemma. The spherical-leaf specialisation is proved in full in Calegari Theorem 4.5 (with Lemma 4.24) and in Mrowka §§23.2–23.6; the general finite-fundamental-group form is stated in Gabai's commentary Theorem 0.8(a) and in the standard reference literature. The complete proof route is the one recorded in the item's strategy.

sources.title: Danny Calegari, Foliations and the Geometry of 3-Manifolds (Oxford Mathematical Monographs; complete author-hosted PDF)
sources.locator: §4.2, printed pp. 140–143 (PDF pp. 149–152) in full; §4.3, printed pp. 144–145 (PDF pp. 153–154), Example 4.7; Lemma 4.24 with proof, printed p. 155 (PDF p. 164)
sources.reading_verification: Downloaded the complete 371-page author-hosted book PDF and extracted it with mutool. Read §4.2 'Foliated bundles and holonomy' end to end on printed pp. 140–143: Example 4.2 (foliated circle bundles and unique path lifting), Theorem 4.3 (complete foliated bundles and representations), the construction of the holonomy representation via the unit normal disk bundle, holonomy transport along a chart chain with its homotopy-invariance argument, Theorem 4.4 (transport is a homomorphism to the groupoid of germs), Theorem 4.5 (Reeb stability for co-oriented foliations with a spherical leaf) with its complete proof — trivial holonomy from π1(λ)=1, openness of the set of spherical leaves, the Novikov limit argument for closedness via H₂(M;Q) finite-dimensionality and co-oriented intersections, and the final gluing h: L×γ→M — and the Remark attributing closedness of the closed-leaf set to Novikov. Read §4.3 Example 4.7 (Reeb component as the quotient of the upper half-space minus the origin by the dilation p↦2p) and the opening of Examples 4.8–4.10 (spiral leaves, spinning, smooth filling). Read Lemma 4.24 with its proof on printed p. 155 (a non-closed leaf meets an embedded transverse circle).

contents.name: Example 4.2, foliated circle bundles; representation ↔ bundle correspondence and unique path lifting (printed pp. 140–141)
contents.support: The quotient-foliation construction used by the mapping torus proposition is the same quotient of a product by a deck action.

contents.name: Theorem 4.3, complete foliated bundles ↔ conjugacy classes of representations (printed p. 141)
contents.reason: Completeness of foliated bundles and the classification of complete bundles are not used; the pair builds the suspension/mapping torus foliation and its holonomy, not the complete-bundle classification.

contents.name: Holonomy representation via the normal disk bundle; transversals and the germ of the return map (printed p. 141)
contents.support: The transverse transport used to build the model map Φ is this construction.

contents.name: Holonomy transport along a chart chain; independence of the chain and of intermediate transversals (printed pp. 141–142)
contents.support: This is the DT-29 supplier interface, consumed here for the model map.

contents.name: Theorem 4.4, holonomy transport is a homomorphism to the groupoid of germs (printed p. 142)
contents.support: Multiplicativity is used for the equivariance of Φ.

contents.name: Theorem 4.5, Reeb stability for co-oriented foliations with a spherical leaf, with complete proof (openness, Novikov closedness, final gluing) (printed pp. 142–143)
contents.support: The spherical-leaf specialisation of the global theorem, with its closedness method (Novikov limit argument) reused in the limit lemma.

contents.name: Remark after Theorem 4.5: closedness of the set of closed leaves, preserved under finite covers, due to Novikov (printed p. 143)
contents.support: Closedness of the compact-leaf set is the first half of the limit lemma.

contents.name: Lemma 4.24 with proof: a non-closed leaf of a codimension-one foliation meets an embedded circle transverse to the foliation (printed p. 155)
Example 4.7, the Reeb component as the quotient of the upper half-space minus the origin by a properly discontinuous dilation; horizontal foliation descends (printed p. 144)
contents.support: This is the quotient model of the Reeb component; the pair uses the equivalent explicit submersion model on the solid cylinder.

contents.name: Examples 4.8–4.10, spiral leaves, spinning, smooth filling of foliated solid tori (printed pp. 144–147)
contents.reason: Three-dimensional foliation engineering and Dehn surgery descriptions are not needed: the explicit quotient model of the solid torus and the two-torus gluing give the Reeb component and the Reeb foliation of S³.

contents.name: Example 4.6, harmonic measure and averaging of transverse measures (printed p. 143)
contents.reason: Invariant transverse measures and their harmonicity belong to the tautness and Godbillon–Vey pair (DT-31); no stability item of this pair uses transverse measures.

contents.name: §4.4, taut foliations: Definition 4.25 and Lemma 4.26 on a single closed transversal (printed pp. 155–156)
contents.reason: Tautness and the single-transversal criterion are the subject of the codimension-one secondary-class pair; the global stability theorem of this pair only needs closedness of the compact-leaf set.

contents.name: §4.4, dead-end components and volume-preserving flows (printed pp. 156–160)
contents.reason: Dead ends and the dynamical characterization of tautness belong to DT-31 and are not consumed by any stability item.

contents.name: Definition 23.1, transversally orientable codimension-one foliation (PDF p. 55)

contents.support: Independent statement and proof strategy for the spherical-leaf specialisation of the global theorem.

contents.name: Remark 7, the free involution (x,θ)↦(−x,−θ) on S²×S¹: the descended foliation is not normally oriented and has two projective-plane leaves (PDF p. 55)
